Faculty Game Overview Guide
What students experience, how the adaptive engine responds, and what faculty should know before assigning a game.

Current architecture: Composer-generated games are self-contained browser HTML files. Official themes and optional faculty images are embedded in the package; Concept Review routing is embedded in the game, while the PDFs stay in the Mastery Quests web library. Progress and run data stay in local browser storage and are not automatically sent to Mastery Quests.
1. The learning model

Mastery Quests combines retrieval practice, mode-specific feedback, adaptive question selection, staged support after errors, escalating difficulty, checkpoint encounters, and Mastery Report. When warranted, the report connects a meaningful weakness to a targeted one-page Concept Review before the student returns to practice.
Correct answers move the learner forward and contribute evidence about concepts, skills, and question forms.
Misses can trigger targeted repair, bridge, and retest questions when the mode and bank support them.
The selector limits recent repeats and uses the available metadata to keep the next item instructionally relevant.
Checkpoint questions test readiness at major milestones without confining ordinary concepts to a single stage.
2. The ten modes
Mode
What changes
When to use it
Standard Campaign
A 30-room campaign with checkpoints, milestones, setbacks, and browser-local save/resume.
Use for the complete game experience.
Timed Trial
A ten-minute run with a visible countdown and no checkpoints; the timer governs completion.
Use for fluency practice after students know the material.
Exam Drill
Adaptive nine-question sections with review and revision before checkpoint commitment; correctness stays hidden while a section is active.
Use for section-based review and deliberate answer commitment.
Legendary Mode
A 30-room campaign using mastery-level, multi-step questions with close choices and no normal remediation sequence.
Use as a later challenge after ordinary mastery is stable.
Score Attack
A scored run rewarding correct answers, speed, and streaks while penalizing misses and rapid guessing.
Use for repeat practice and motivation, not first exposure.
Quiz
A fixed run of 1-15 questions chosen by the student while faculty-selected concepts remain fixed.
Use when assigning a specific-length classroom or homework run.
Unlimited Practice
Adaptive practice repeats in 30-question cycles until the student ends the session and generates a report.
Use for open-ended practice where students decide when to stop.
Trial by Graph
A 10-, 15-, or 20-question run using only audited items in which the graph is required; only supported lengths appear.
Use for concentrated graphical-analysis practice.
Fading Fortune
A 10-, 15-, or 20-question run. Random incorrect choices fade at difficulty-based intervals and value falls 100 -> 75 -> 50 -> 25.
Use for time pressure without a full-run clock.
Risk & Reward
A 10-, 15-, or 20-question run with a 1,000-point bankroll. Students risk 10%, 25%, 50%, or all in before seeing each question.
Use for strategic confidence-and-stakes decisions.
3. What happens after a wrong answer

In supported modes, the engine can route the learner into a short remediation sequence tied to the missed concept or skill. A correct repair can lead to a bridge or retest before ordinary progression resumes. When no appropriate repair route exists, the engine applies the normal room setback instead. Legendary Mode intentionally removes the staged repair sequence.
4. Checkpoints and progression

The visible path uses three checkpoints. The composer maps published easy checkpoint questions to Checkpoint One, medium checkpoint questions to Checkpoint Two, and hard checkpoint questions to the Final Checkpoint. Optional checkpoint focus narrows eligible concepts for a checkpoint; it does not remove those concepts from ordinary question selection.
5. Mastery Report and Concept Reviews

Mastery Report summarizes the evidence from the run and identifies the strongest and weakest signals across concepts or learning objectives and, where applicable, question forms or skills. It is diagnostic evidence, not a replacement for an aligned exam, and low-evidence runs should be interpreted cautiously.

The production library provides one-page reviews across General Economics, Microeconomics, and Macroeconomics. Generated games embed only the routing they need; the PDFs stay centrally hosted in the Mastery Quests web library.

When a meaningful weakness maps to an available review, the report can recommend the corresponding one-page Concept Review. A clean run may produce no recommendation. The student opens the PDF, reviews the core idea and worked example, then returns to targeted practice, Repair, or Bridge so later performance creates new evidence.
A high Score Attack total or fast completion is not the same thing as broad mastery.
6. Saving, Concept Reviews, and privacy
The game can store the player name or initials, mode state, progress, local results, mastery evidence, and preferences in that browser.

Standard Campaign and Legendary Mode support browser-local save/resume. Timed Trial, Exam Drill, Quiz, Unlimited Practice, Score Attack, Trial by Graph, Fading Fortune, and Risk & Reward attempts do not resume after leaving the run.

Composer-generated games do not request a school email and do not automatically transmit gameplay data to a Mastery Quests server. Separate classroom research builds may collect anonymous measurements; use their course or study notice instead of assuming the public workflow.
If a course requires a downloaded CSV, screenshot, verification code, or mastery report, the student submits that evidence deliberately through the instructor’s chosen LMS or course workflow.
Clearing browser site data or switching devices can remove locally stored progress.

Assign a specific mode rather than telling students simply to “play the game.”

Purpose. This helper gives faculty the structure needed to create clean, engine-ready question-bank items. Draft questions in a table, audit the bank, and only then convert each row into JavaScript objects.

Core rule. Every item needs a unique ID, question text, four options, a correct-answer index, a consistent tag and type, and feedback that teaches. New banks should also include an explicit objective and micro-skill metadata so the current engine can target repair, bridge, retest, boss selection, and mastery reporting accurately.
Unique identifier. Never reuse it anywhere in the package.
Correct option before the engine shuffles choices. Counting starts at 0.
Broad content area used for adaptive tracking and reporting.

Brief explanation or correction shown after answering.
Exact course or textbook learning objective.
Precise micro-skill the item directly tests. This is the main repair and mastery key.
Skill route used when the best recovery target differs from the item label. Often matches primarySkill.
Specific misconception exposed by a wrong answer. Useful for bridge and diagnostic routing.
Instructional role or bank level. Keep it aligned with the pool that contains the item.
Groups related objectives or skills for broader analysis.
Additional skills involved, but not the main target.
Exact filename of a graph, table, or diagram displayed with the item.
Short pre-answer cue when that game version supports hints.
Marks whether the visual is necessary to answer the item. Trial by Graph uses only items marked true.
Tag = broad area. Use a stable topic such as elasticity, taxation, production, monetary_policy, or agency_costs.
Objective = formal outcome. Use the exact course or textbook code that faculty and students recognize, such as LO5.2.
Primary skill = precise task. Name the smallest useful skill the engine should target, such as midpoint_elasticity_calculation or identify_demand_shifter.
Common error = misconception. Name the wrong reasoning pattern, not merely wrong_answer. Good metadata tells the engine what broke. Bad metadata just shrugs.
The “a” field uses zero-based numbering before answer choices are shuffled. The correct answer is identified by a. For example, if the correct answer is the third option, then use a: 2.
Do not write every item at the same level and dump it into one pile. The engine uses different pools for different instructional jobs.
Build retrieval, interpretation, calculation, and application with increasing complexity.
Stretch strong students with multi-step, integration, trap, and synthesis items.
Provide checkpoint sets with enough objective, type, and skill variety to avoid stale or repetitive battles.
Use a simpler one-step item that isolates the broken micro-skill. Repair is not a disguised duplicate of the missed question.
Require the student to apply the repaired idea in a nearby diagnostic or transfer situation.
Return to an appropriate main-bank item tied to the same skill or objective.
Use mastery-level questions with close alternatives and multi-step reasoning. Legendary mode does not use normal remediation.

Common ID convention. Many current builds reserve 1-99 for easy, 100-199 for medium, 200-299 for hard, 300-399 for elite, 2000+/3000+/4000+ for boss pools, 5000+ for repair, 6000+ for bridge, and 9000+ for legendary items. Some full builds also use 30000+ for direct core-skill repair seeds. Follow the ranges already established in the game you are editing. Do not invent a second numbering system inside the same file.
Use the exact filename and extension referenced by the image field. Current game packages commonly use .webp, though .png and .jpg can work when the path matches.
Keep filenames lowercase and simple. Use underscores instead of spaces.
Place the image in the same published folder as index.html unless the code deliberately uses a subfolder path.
Make the prompt identify what students must read from the visual. The standard engine supplies generic graph accessibility text; essential information should not depend on color alone.
Test the normal display, enlarged lightbox, mobile view, and published GitHub Pages version. A graph that works only on your desktop is not working.
Troubleshooting. Check filename, capitalization, extension, and folder location first. Most missing-image mysteries are basic path mistakes wearing a dramatic cape.

using-external-javascript-question-pools: USING EXTERNAL JAVASCRIPTQUESTION POOLS
Moving question content out of the Version 4 HTML engine without breaking the game

Bottom lineAn external JavaScript file separates the question bank from the game engine. It makes large banks easier to maintain, but it does not simplify the question-writing work and it does not hide answers from students.
1. What an external question pool changes

The standard faculty template stores the question bank inside the HTML file. That is the safest setup for a single game because faculty can download one file, replace the content, and publish it. An external JavaScript question pool moves the content declarations into a separate .js file while leaving the interface and engine in the HTML file.

The browser still loads both files. The difference is organizational: the HTML contains the engine, while the JavaScript file contains the authored questions, learning-objective labels, and remediation pools.
Embedded bank
External JavaScript bank
One main HTML file contains engine and content.
The HTML engine and question content are maintained as separate files.
Simplest option for first-time users and one-off games.
Cleaner option for large banks, repeated revisions, and shared content workflows.
Fewer file-path problems.
Requires correct filename, location, load order, and publishing.
Editing can become unwieldy when the bank is large.
Question writers can work in the bank file without touching most engine code.
2. When to use it
Use an external pool when
The question bank is large enough that the HTML file is difficult to navigate.
Several people will revise question content while one person protects the engine.
You want to replace or update content without scrolling through the full engine.
You are maintaining several related games and need a cleaner content workflow.
You understand basic file paths and can test the published version before launch.
Keep the bank embedded when
You are building one game and only need to replace the supplied questions.
The faculty member is uncomfortable managing multiple files.
The game will be copied frequently and missing-file mistakes are likely.
There is no clear benefit beyond making the repository look more complicated.
3. Recommended folder structure
Keep the HTML game and its JavaScript question pool in the same game folder unless you deliberately configure another path. Boring paths work. Clever paths create support tickets.
Single-game foldercourse-game/|-- index.html|-- question_bank.js|-- graph_1.webp|-- graph_2.webp
For a course hub, place each game in its own subfolder. Each game may have its own question_bank.js file.
Hub with separate gamescourse-hub/|-- index.html                 // multi-game hub|-- game-1/|   |-- index.html|   |-- question_bank.js|-- game-2/|   |-- index.html|   |-- question_bank.js

Same-origin ruleThe hub and games should be published from the same GitHub Pages site or web origin if they are expected to share browser progress. External question pools should also be served from that same site.
4. What belongs in question_bank.js

The exact content block depends on the game template. In the current Version 4 engine, the external file should contain the authored data declarations. Engine-generated routing functions should remain in the HTML file.
Move to question_bank.js
Keep in index.html

microSkillBridgePools
Progression, boss, mode, scoring, save, telemetry, and mastery-report logic

A minimal faculty template may use only questionBanks and objectiveLabels. A full game may also include repair and bridge pools. Do not invent empty replacements for content structures that the engine expects to use.
Basic external file pattern

// question_bank.js// Do not add <script> tags, Markdown fences, import, or export.const questionBanks = {  easy: [],  medium: [],  hard: [],  elite: [],  legendary: [],  easyBoss: [],  mediumBoss: [],  finalBoss: [],  legendaryBoss: []};const objectiveLabels = {  "LO1.1": "Replace with a readable objective label"};const microSkillRepairPools = {};const skillRepairSeedPools = {};const microSkillBridgePools = {};
5. Connect the external file to the HTML engine
Step 1: Create the JavaScript file
1. Create a plain-text file named question_bank.js.
2. Paste the required data declarations into the file.
3. Remove all HTML script tags and any Markdown code fences. A .js file contains JavaScript only.
4. Save the file in the same folder as index.html unless the script path says otherwise.
Step 2: Load it before the engine
Place this line immediately before the main engine script. Use a normal classic script. Do not add type="module" and do not add async.
<script src="question_bank.js"></script><script>  // Version 4 engine begins here</script>
Load order mattersThe question-bank file must finish loading before the engine runs. async can reverse the order. type="module" changes scope and loading behavior. Neither belongs in the basic setup.
Step 3: Remove duplicate declarations from index.html

Delete the embedded declarations that were moved into question_bank.js. Leave the surrounding engine logic alone. If questionBanks remains declared in both files, the browser will stop with a duplicate-identifier error.

Remove from index.html:const questionBanks = { ... };const objectiveLabels = { ... };const microSkillRepairPools = { ... };const skillRepairSeedPools = { ... };const microSkillBridgePools = { ... };Keep in index.html:Object.assign(microSkillRepairPools, skillRepairSeedPools);function buildDirectSkillRepairRoutes(){ ... }const directSkillRepairRoutes = buildDirectSkillRepairRoutes();
6. Question-file rules that still apply
Externalizing the bank changes the file location, not the question standard. Every item still needs valid JavaScript syntax and the metadata required by the engine.
Every ID is unique across routine, boss, elite, Legendary, repair, and bridge pools.
Every question has exactly four options and a zero-based correct-answer index from 0 to 3.
Tags, types, objectives, primarySkill, repairSkill, commonError, conceptCluster, and difficulty values use consistent spelling.
Image filenames and capitalization match the uploaded files exactly.
Feedback explains the reasoning instead of merely announcing the correct letter.
The bank is audited for duplicate wording, answer accuracy, weak distractors, and answer-length bias.

Do not convert the file to JSONThe current engine expects JavaScript declarations, not raw JSON. JSON cannot contain const declarations and cannot be loaded with a normal script tag as a question bank.
7. Publishing and testing
GitHub Pages
1. Upload index.html and question_bank.js to the same game folder.
2. Confirm that GitHub shows the exact filename and capitalization used by the script tag.
3. Wait for GitHub Pages to rebuild.
4. Open the published game and perform a hard refresh after replacing the question bank.
5. Use the browser Network panel to confirm that question_bank.js loads with status 200 rather than 404.
